Work mode, salary, and education: what the data says

A client-facing view of the completed analysis, focused on compensation patterns, remote versus hybrid work, and salary differences across education groups. All numerical results below are synchronized with the final Jupyter notebook.

Executive summary

Key takeaways for the client

The analysis highlights three main patterns: Remote respondents have higher observed annual salaries than Hybrid respondents; mean salary is not the same across all three education groups in the North American sample; and compensation is highly right-skewed, so high-end values can noticeably influence averages.

Question 1

Exploratory data analysis

Three requested views of job satisfaction, mean salary by job title, and salary versus age, with anomalies called out explicitly.

Average job satisfaction by job title

Invalid JobSat = 60 was excluded because the valid scale is 0–10.

Average satisfaction is generally clustered around 7–8. The retired category reaches 10, but that estimate is based on only one valid response and should be interpreted cautiously.

Mean annual salary by job title

Upper-tail compensation strongly affects the mean for some small groups.

Financial analysts/engineers have the highest mean at about $501k, driven heavily by an extreme $18.4M salary in a relatively small group. Very small categories such as retired respondents also require caution.

Annual salary versus age

Five clearly implausible ages (1, 3, 9, 126 and 151) plus 10 missing ages were excluded from this figure.

Salary generally rises from younger to middle-aged respondents but remains highly dispersed, with extreme high-income observations. The much smaller number of older respondents makes patterns at high ages less stable.

Outlier assessment

Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, 403 Hybrid salaries (5.16%) and 204 Remote salaries (2.94%) were flagged as potential outliers.

They were retained because salary is strongly right-skewed and very high salaries can be legitimate observations rather than data errors.

Bootstrap mean-salary analysis

10,000 resamples, with each work mode resampled at its original group size. Use the tabs to switch among the three required figures.

Bootstrap centers: Hybrid $101,811.95; Remote $118,748.15. The Remote sampling distribution is centered higher and is somewhat more dispersed.
The bootstrap mean difference is about −$16,936, very close to the observed −$16,894. Most resampled differences are below zero.
After standardization, the distribution has mean ≈ 0 and SD ≈ 1. Standardization changes center and scale, not shape.

95% confidence intervals

Welch t-based CI(-$29,856.10, -$3,930.91)
Bootstrap percentile CI(-$31,102.27, -$4,883.75)

Neither interval includes zero, so both approaches support a difference in population mean salary, with Remote higher on the observed scale.

Bootstrap education analysis

10,000 replications using original group sample sizes. Use the tabs to switch among the three required figures.

Bootstrap mean centers: Bachelor's $161,024.86; Master's $182,202.36; Professional $197,530.32. The Professional distribution is widest, consistent with its smaller sample and larger raw SD.
Bootstrap centers: Bachelor's−Master's ≈ −$21,178; Bachelor's−Professional ≈ −$36,505; Master's−Professional ≈ −$15,328. The Master's−Professional distribution is wider and crosses zero.
Each standardized distribution has mean ≈ 0 and SD ≈ 1, making their shapes directly comparable.
Bootstrap ANOVA: the observed F-statistic is 17.4966. In 10,000 null bootstrap replications, none produced an F-statistic at least this large. With the finite-bootstrap +1 correction, p ≈ 0.0001, agreeing with the original ANOVA conclusion.
Methodology & interpretation

How to read the results

Plain-language explanations of the statistical tools used in the notebook.

What does a p-value mean here?

A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true.

What does bootstrapping do?

Bootstrapping repeatedly resamples the observed data with replacement to approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic. The analysis uses 10,000 replications and the original group sample sizes.

Why keep potential salary outliers?

Compensation is strongly right-skewed, and very high salaries can be legitimate. IQR rules flag statistical extremes, not necessarily errors. Without direct evidence of data-entry problems, the analysis retains these observations.

Why use Welch tests as robustness checks?

Observed group standard deviations differ, and group sizes are unequal. Welch procedures do not require equal population variances, so agreement with the pooled/standard ANOVA results strengthens the robustness of the conclusion.
